# Information, Signals, and Markets {#information}

Why does a used-car dealer offer a 12-month warranty it hopes never to honour? Why
do start-ups pay premium fees to be underwritten by prestigious investment banks,
and why do some of the wealthiest consumers buy handbags with *no* visible logo?
Each puzzle has the same structure. One party knows something valuable — the
quality of a car, the prospects of a firm, the wealth of a buyer — and another
party cannot observe it directly. The informed party therefore *does* something
observable that the uninformed party can use to infer what is hidden.

This chapter introduces the family of theories that explain how markets,
organizations, and people cope with **information asymmetry**. We begin with the
problem itself (Akerlof's "lemons"), then develop **signaling theory**, its mirror
image **screening theory**, the biology-inspired idea of **costly signaling**, and
two consumer-behaviour extensions — **identity signaling** and **countersignaling**.
Together they form one of the most widely used theoretical toolkits in
management, marketing, finance, and economics.

```{r tab-sig-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "Information asymmetry", "What happens when one side of a transaction knows more?", "Market / dyad", "Akerlof (1970)",
  "Signaling theory", "How can the informed party credibly reveal hidden quality?", "Dyad / market", "Spence (1973)",
  "Screening theory", "How can the uninformed party induce disclosure?", "Dyad / market", "Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976)",
  "Costly signaling", "Why must honest signals be expensive to fake?", "Individual / population", "Zahavi (1975)",
  "Identity signaling", "Why do consumers converge or diverge in their choices?", "Individual / group", "Berger & Heath (2007)",
  "Countersignaling", "Why do the highest types sometimes refuse to signal?", "Individual / market", "Feltovich et al. (2002)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of information and signals.")
```

## Information Asymmetry {#information-asymmetry}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When sellers know more about quality than buyers, buyers pay only
for *average* quality; high-quality sellers withdraw, average quality falls, and
the market can unravel.

**Origins.** Economics; @akerlof1970, building on earlier work on uncertainty and
insurance. Akerlof, Spence, and Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel Memorial Prize in
Economic Sciences for analyses of markets with asymmetric information.

**Level of analysis.** Market and dyad (buyer–seller, investor–firm,
employer–applicant).

**Key constructs.** Hidden information (adverse selection); hidden action (moral
hazard); quality uncertainty; pooling.

**Boundary conditions.** Quality is unobservable *before* purchase, is costly to
verify, and matters to the buyer; no cheap third-party verification exists.

**Related theories.** [Signaling](#signaling-theory), [Screening](#screening-theory),
[Agency theory](#agency-theory), [Transaction cost economics](#transaction-cost-economics).
:::

### Core logic

@akerlof1970 used the market for used cars to show how hidden quality can destroy
a market. Suppose half of the cars are good ("peaches") and half are bad
("lemons"). Buyers cannot tell them apart, so they are willing to pay only the
expected value of a random car. Owners of good cars find that price too low and
keep their cars; the share of lemons in the market rises; buyers anticipate this
and lower their offers further. In the limit, only lemons trade. The general
lesson is that **adverse selection** — the tendency of hidden-information markets
to attract the "wrong" types — can make mutually beneficial trades disappear.

Economists distinguish two forms of asymmetry
[@stiglitz2000; @connelly2010]:

```{r tab-sig-types}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Dimension, ~`Hidden information`, ~`Hidden action`,
  "Also called", "Adverse selection", "Moral hazard",
  "What is hidden", "A characteristic (quality, ability, risk type)", "Behaviour after contracting (effort, care)",
  "Timing", "Before the transaction", "After the transaction",
  "Classic example", "Used-car quality; applicant ability", "Insured driver's care; manager's effort",
  "Typical remedy", "Signals, screens, certification, warranties", "Monitoring, incentives, bonding",
  "Home theory", "Signaling / screening theory", "Agency theory"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Two forms of information asymmetry.")
```

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sig-lemons) simulates the unravelling process. Quality is
uniformly distributed, buyers value a car at 1.2 times its quality, and sellers
only sell if the price is at least their car's quality. Each round, buyers offer
the expected value of the cars that remain on the market. The market shrinks
round after round.

```{r fig-sig-lemons, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of Akerlof's lemons problem: when buyers can only pay for average quality, the best sellers exit and the market shrinks.", fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(2001)
q <- runif(5000, 0, 100)                     # seller quality (private information)
price <- 1.2 * mean(q)                       # round 1: buyers pay for average quality
rounds <- vector("list", 8)
for (r in 1:8) {
  on_market <- q[q <= price]                 # sellers with quality above price withdraw
  rounds[[r]] <- data.frame(round = r, share = length(on_market) / length(q),
                            avg_quality = mean(on_market), price = price)
  price <- 1.2 * mean(on_market)             # buyers update to the new average
}
lemons <- bind_rows(rounds)
ggplot(lemons, aes(round, share)) +
  geom_col(fill = pal[["blue"]], width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, 1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1.08), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Round of price adjustment", y = "Share of cars still offered",
       title = "Adverse selection unravels the market",
       subtitle = "Buyers value cars at 1.2x quality but can observe only the market average",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (n = 5,000 sellers, quality ~ Uniform[0, 100]).")
```

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Certified pre-owned programs.** The used-car market is the textbook lemons
market, and the industry's best-known response is the manufacturer-backed
*certified pre-owned* (CPO) program: a multi-point inspection plus an extended
warranty. Both elements attack the asymmetry directly — inspection converts hidden
information into verifiable information, and the warranty makes a low-quality car
expensive for the *seller* to certify. Similar logic underlies home-inspection
contingencies in real estate, escrow services in online marketplaces, and
"satisfaction guaranteed" return policies in retailing.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Mandatory disclosure.** Information can also be disclosed by regulation. When Los
Angeles County required restaurants to post hygiene grade cards in their windows,
health inspection scores rose and foodborne-illness hospitalizations fell
[@jin2003]. A hidden attribute (kitchen hygiene) became a visible one, and
consumers and restaurants both responded. See @dranove2010 for a review of
disclosure and certification.
:::

## Signaling Theory {#signaling-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** An informed party (the *signaler*) can credibly convey unobservable
quality by taking a costly, observable action that low-quality types would find
too expensive to imitate.

**Origins.** Labour economics; @spence1973 on education as a job-market signal;
reviewed in @spence2002 and, for management, @connelly2010.

**Level of analysis.** Dyad and market: job applicant–employer, firm–investor,
brand–consumer, start-up–venture capitalist.

**Key constructs.** Signaler; receiver; signal; signal cost; signal fit;
signal observability; signal consistency; separating vs. pooling equilibrium;
feedback (countersignals).

**Boundary conditions.** Quality is unobservable *ex ante*; the cost of the signal
is *negatively correlated with quality*; receivers can observe the signal and
know (or learn) how to interpret it.

**Related theories.** [Information asymmetry](#information-asymmetry),
[Screening](#screening-theory), [Costly signaling](#costly-signaling),
[Agency theory](#agency-theory), [Institutional theory](#institutional-theory).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@spence1973 asked why employers pay more to workers with more education even if
education teaches nothing productive. His answer: education is a **signal**.
If acquiring a degree is less costly — in effort, time, or psychic cost — for
high-ability people, then only high-ability people will find it worthwhile to
acquire it, and employers can rationally use the degree to sort applicants. The
signal need not *create* the quality it reveals; it only needs to be harder to
obtain for those who lack it.

The idea spread quickly. In finance, debt levels and dividends were modelled as
signals of managers' private information [@ross1977; @bhattacharya1979;
@myers1984]. In marketing, advertising spending, price, warranties, and brand
names were analysed as signals of unobservable product quality [@nelson1974;
@milgrom1986; @kirmani1989; @boulding1993; @erdem1998; @kirmani2000]. In
management, signaling theory became a standard lens for IPOs, board composition,
corporate social responsibility, and the hiring process [@certo2003;
@connelly2010; @bergh2014].

### Core logic and propositions

@connelly2010 organize signaling theory around a timeline with four elements.
Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sig-timeline) redraws that logic.

```{r fig-sig-timeline, fig.cap = "The signaling timeline: a signaler with private information sends a signal; the receiver observes and interprets it, chooses an action, and may send feedback. Adapted from the framework in Connelly et al. (2011)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  S  [label = "Signaler\\n(insider with private\\ninformation about quality)", %s]
  G  [label = "Signal\\n(costly, observable\\naction)", %s]
  R  [label = "Receiver\\n(outsider who lacks\\ninformation)", %s]
  A  [label = "Receiver action\\n(hire, invest, buy)", %s]
  E  [label = "Signaling\\nenvironment\\n(noise, distortion)", %s]
  S -> G [label = " sends"]
  G -> R [label = " observes &\\n interprets"]
  R -> A [label = " chooses"]
  A -> S [label = " feedback", style = dashed, constraint = false]
  E -> G [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_construct, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

Formally, a signal is informative when it supports a **separating equilibrium** —
different types choose different signals, so the receiver can infer type from the
signal. When all types send the same signal, the equilibrium is **pooling** and
the signal carries no information. The theory's central propositions can be
stated as follows:

- **P1 (Differential cost).** A signal separates types only if its cost is lower
  for high-quality than for low-quality signalers (the *single-crossing*
  condition).
- **P2 (Observability).** The more observable a signal is to receivers, the
  stronger its effect on receiver beliefs [@connelly2010].
- **P3 (Fit).** Signals are more effective when they are logically connected to the
  unobservable quality being signalled (e.g., a warranty fits durability; a
  celebrity endorsement fits less well).
- **P4 (Consistency).** Consistent signals across time and channels are more
  credible than one-off or conflicting signals.
- **P5 (Receiver attention and interpretation).** Signal effects depend on whether
  receivers attend to the signal and on how they calibrate it; signals are
  socially interpreted, not mechanically decoded.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sig-separating) shows the single-crossing logic for Spence's
education model. Because the high-ability type's cost line is flatter, there is a
range of education levels (shaded) that high types are willing to acquire but low
types are not. Any education requirement in that range separates the two types.

```{r fig-sig-separating, fig.cap = "Stylised Spence model. Education costs more for low-ability workers. A credential level in the shaded range is worth acquiring for high-ability workers (wage premium exceeds cost) but not for low-ability workers, producing a separating equilibrium.", fig.height = 4}
premium <- 40                                  # wage premium paid to signalers
edu <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.05)
cost <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(edu, cost = 8 * edu, type = "Low-ability worker"),
  data.frame(edu, cost = 4 * edu, type = "High-ability worker")
)
lo <- premium / 8; hi <- premium / 4            # separating range: [5, 10]
ggplot(cost, aes(edu, cost, colour = type)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["aqua"]], alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = premium, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.2, y = premium + 3, label = "Wage premium for credential", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.4, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = (lo + hi) / 2, y = 75, label = "Separating\nrange", size = 3.6,
           colour = ink[["primary"]], fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("High-ability worker" = pal[["blue"]], "Low-ability worker" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 85)) +
  labs(x = "Years of education required for the credential", y = "Cost of acquiring the credential",
       colour = NULL, title = "Why education can signal ability",
       caption = "Stylised: cost = 4 x education (high ability), 8 x education (low ability); premium = 40.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The empirical record is large and spans disciplines:

- **Product quality.** Consumers infer quality from warranties [@boulding1993],
  perceived advertising expense [@kirmani1989], and price–advertising combinations
  [@milgrom1986]. @kirmani2000 synthesise this literature and argue that
  "no pain, no gain": signals work when a low-quality firm would lose money by
  sending them.
- **Brands.** @erdem1998 conceptualise **brand equity itself as a signal**: a
  brand is a credible promise because the firm has invested in it and stands to
  lose that investment if it cheats.
- **Capital markets.** Prestigious boards and underwriters are associated with
  better IPO outcomes [@certo2003]. In corporate finance, issuing equity can
  signal that managers believe shares are *over*valued, which helps explain
  negative stock-price reactions to equity issues [@myers1984].
- **Management research.** @bergh2014 note that many studies assume rather than
  test the differential-cost condition, and call for research on equilibrium:
  whether signals actually separate types in the population studied.

::: {.debate}
**Is it really a signal?** Many papers label any observable firm attribute a
"signal". Critics argue that a variable is a signal in the theoretical sense only
if (a) it is chosen by the signaler, (b) its cost differs by type, and (c) it
changes receiver beliefs. Without evidence on (b), a "signal" may simply be a
correlate of quality, and the theory is doing little explanatory work
[@bergh2014]. A second debate concerns the *human capital* alternative: education
may raise productivity and also signal it; separating these explanations requires
careful designs (e.g., sheepskin effects, natural experiments).
:::

### Applications in business

Signals appear in every business function. Table \@ref(tab:tab-sig-business)
maps common signals to the hidden attributes they communicate.

```{r tab-sig-business}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Function, ~Signaler, ~`Hidden attribute`, ~Signal, ~`Why it is costly to fake`,
  "Marketing", "Manufacturer", "Product durability", "Long warranty", "Low-quality products generate expensive claims",
  "Marketing", "New brand", "Quality and staying power", "Heavy launch advertising", "Spend is recouped only through repeat purchase",
  "Finance", "IPO firm", "Firm prospects", "Prestigious underwriter / board", "Reputational intermediaries screen and risk their name",
  "Finance", "Mature firm", "Stable cash flows", "Regular dividends", "Cutting dividends later is penalised",
  "HR", "Job applicant", "Ability and diligence", "Degree; certifications", "Harder to complete for lower-ability candidates",
  "HR", "Employer", "Good workplace", "Employer awards; transparent pay", "Audits and employee reviews expose false claims",
  "Strategy", "Incumbent", "Resolve to fight entry", "Capacity investment", "Sunk costs are lost if the firm retreats",
  "Platforms", "Seller", "Reliability", "Verified badges; long review history", "Reputation takes time to build and is lost by cheating"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Signals across business functions.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Venture funding and the start-up signaling stack.** An early-stage start-up has
little revenue history, so investors rely heavily on signals: the founders'
track records, affiliation with selective accelerators, patents, and the identity
of earlier investors. Each signal is costly to obtain for a weak venture — an
accelerator screens out most applicants; a top-tier lead investor stakes its
reputation. A practical implication for founders is **signal fit**: patents are a
strong signal of technical novelty but a weak signal of go-to-market ability,
whereas paying pilot customers signal demand. Investors, in turn, should ask
whether a signal is *differentially* costly — a polished pitch deck is not.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: warranty design.** A mid-market appliance maker has a
lower failure rate than its rivals but cannot convince retailers. Moving from a
one-year to a five-year warranty is a credible signal precisely because it would
bankrupt a firm with a high failure rate. A back-of-the-envelope test: expected
warranty cost per unit = failure probability × repair cost × years covered. If
that cost is small for the focal firm but large for imitators, the warranty
separates; if every competitor can match it cheaply, the warranty will be copied
and the market will pool.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms that offer longer warranties will receive higher consumer quality
  ratings, and this effect will be stronger for experience goods than for search goods.
- *H2.* The positive effect of underwriter prestige on IPO valuation will be weaker
  when analyst coverage of the industry is high (lower information asymmetry).
- *H3.* Signal consistency (low variance across third-party ratings) will
  strengthen the effect of average rating on sales.

**Designs.** Field data with plausibly exogenous variation in signal cost (policy
changes, certification thresholds); regression discontinuity around rating
cut-offs; lab or online experiments manipulating signal presence and cost;
structural models that estimate types and equilibria.

**Measures.** Signal cost (spend, warranty length, credential difficulty);
observability (media mentions, prominence); receiver response (price, choice,
valuation, hiring); information asymmetry (analyst dispersion, firm age,
intangibles ratio).

**Contexts.** IPOs and crowdfunding; online marketplaces and reviews; hiring and
credentials; ESG disclosure; product launches.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating every attribute as a signal.** Theory requires that the signal be
*chosen* and *differentially costly*. If you cannot argue — and ideally show —
that low-quality signalers would find the signal more expensive, you are probably
studying a correlate of quality, not a signal. State the cost structure
explicitly and test for heterogeneity in signal effects across levels of
information asymmetry.
:::

## Screening Theory {#screening-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When the uninformed party moves first, it can design a menu of
contracts that induces informed parties to *self-select*, revealing their type
through the option they choose.

**Origins.** Insurance economics; @rothschild1976; @stiglitz2000.

**Level of analysis.** Dyad and market (insurer–insured, lender–borrower,
employer–applicant, firm–customer).

**Key constructs.** Self-selection; incentive compatibility; menu of contracts;
information rents.

**Boundary conditions.** The uninformed party can commit to a menu; types differ
in preferences or costs in a way the menu can exploit.

**Related theories.** [Signaling](#signaling-theory), [Agency theory](#agency-theory).
:::

Signaling and screening are mirror images. In **signaling**, the informed party
moves first; in **screening**, the uninformed party moves first by offering
choices. An insurer that offers both a low-premium/high-deductible plan and a
high-premium/low-deductible plan lets customers sort themselves: low-risk drivers
prefer the high deductible because they expect few claims [@rothschild1976].

```{r tab-sig-vs-screen}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~Signaling, ~Screening,
  "Who moves first", "Informed party (signaler)", "Uninformed party (screener)",
  "Instrument", "Costly action or credential", "Menu of contracts or options",
  "Revelation through", "Choice of signal", "Self-selection among options",
  "Classic model", "Spence (1973) job market", "Rothschild & Stiglitz (1976) insurance",
  "Business examples", "Warranties, degrees, certifications", "Deductibles, versioning, probation periods, freemium tiers"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Signaling versus screening.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Versioning and freemium.** Software firms routinely screen customers by offering
tiers — a free plan with limits, a professional plan, and an enterprise plan with
security and compliance features. Customers with high willingness to pay
self-select into higher tiers because the features they need are only available
there. The design problem is **incentive compatibility**: each tier must be the
best choice for the segment it targets, or high-value customers will "trade down".
:::

## Costly Signaling {#costly-signaling}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Signals are honest when they are costly in a way only high-quality
senders can afford — the **handicap principle**.

**Origins.** Evolutionary biology [@zahavi1975]; anticipated in economics by
Veblen's analysis of conspicuous consumption [@veblen1899].

**Level of analysis.** Individual (organism or consumer) within a population.

**Key constructs.** Handicap; honest signal; conspicuous consumption; status.

**Related theories.** [Signaling](#signaling-theory), [Snob effect](#snob-effect),
[Identity signaling](#identity-signaling).
:::

@zahavi1975 proposed that the peacock's tail is an honest signal of fitness *because*
it is a handicap: only a healthy bird can survive while carrying it. Veblen had made
a parallel argument about the "leisure class", whose conspicuous waste of time and
money demonstrated wealth [@veblen1899]. In consumer research, costly signaling
explains luxury consumption, charitable giving with public recognition, and
expensive rituals that demonstrate commitment.

As @Berger_2016 puts it, the more costly something is, the more likely it is to
retain its value as a clear signal. Costs need not be monetary: they can be
**time** (mastering an esoteric hobby), **opportunity** (forgoing alternatives), or
**knowledge** (insider tastes that take years to acquire).

## Identity Signaling {#identity-signaling}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Consumers diverge from others in product domains that signal
identity; when outgroups adopt a taste, ingroup members abandon it to avoid
signalling an undesired identity.

**Origins.** Consumer psychology; @Berger_2007; popularised in @Berger_2016.

**Level of analysis.** Individual consumer within social groups.

**Key constructs.** Identity-relevance of the domain; observability; outgroup
adoption; misidentification cost.

**Related theories.** [Optimal distinctiveness](#optimal-distinctiveness-theory),
[Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory), [Snob effect](#snob-effect).
:::

People do not diverge everywhere. @Berger_2007 show that divergence is concentrated
in domains seen as **identity-relevant** — music, clothing, hairstyles, cars —
rather than in functional domains such as dish soap. Two features make a domain
a good identity signal: it is **observable** to others, and it is chosen for its
**symbolic** rather than functional value. When a dissimilar outgroup adopts a
taste, ingroup members abandon it because continued use risks
**misidentification** [@Berger_2007; @Berger_2016].

This produces a cycle that marketers know well: identity signaling causes tastes
to *catch on* within groups and also to *die out* once they diffuse too broadly.
Counterfeits accelerate the cycle by diluting a signal's exclusivity, pushing
early adopters toward the next thing [@Berger_2016].

```{r fig-sig-identity, fig.cap = "Mechanism of identity signaling: outgroup adoption lowers a product's value as an identity signal in observable, identity-relevant domains, prompting ingroup abandonment."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  O [label = "Outgroup adopts\\nthe product", %s]
  M [label = "Signal value falls;\\nmisidentification risk rises", %s]
  D [label = "Ingroup abandons\\nthe product (divergence)", %s]
  X [label = "Identity relevance\\nof the domain", %s]
  V [label = "Observability\\nof use", %s]
  O -> M -> D
  X -> M [style = dashed]
  V -> M [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator, node_moderator))
```

::: {.business-case}
**Managing the fashion cycle.** Brands with strong identity value face a paradox:
growth dilutes the signal that made them attractive. Common responses include
limited editions and "drops" that ration supply, sub-brands for different
segments, and pricing architecture that keeps a flagship line exclusive. Each is a
way of preserving signal value while expanding reach.
:::

## Countersignaling {#countersignaling}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** High types sometimes *avoid* the signal that medium types use,
because they are confident that other information already separates them from
low types.

**Origins.** Economics, @feltovich2002; consumer research on brand prominence,
@han2010.

**Level of analysis.** Individual and market.

**Key constructs.** Low / medium / high types; extraneous information; brand
prominence; "quiet" signals.
:::

@feltovich2002 explain why the most talented students sometimes do not bother to
show off, why the wealthiest dress down, and why the most secure firms forgo
flashy marketing. If receivers have other, noisy information that already sets
high types apart from low types, medium types still need to signal to separate
themselves from low types — but high types can separate from *medium* types by
**not** signaling.

@han2010 found a consumer analogue in luxury goods. They classified consumers by
wealth and need for status. Status-seeking consumers without old wealth
("parvenus") prefer loud, prominently branded goods; wealthy consumers with a low
need for status ("patricians") prefer quiet goods whose subtle cues are recognisable
only to fellow insiders. The result is a non-monotonic relationship between price
and logo prominence, sketched in Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sig-prominence).

```{r fig-sig-prominence, fig.cap = "Stylised relationship between price tier and brand prominence implied by countersignaling: prominence rises with price for status-seeking buyers but falls at the very top, where quiet signals speak only to insiders.", fig.height = 3.8}
tiers <- data.frame(
  tier = factor(c("Mass", "Premium", "Luxury", "Top luxury", "Bespoke"),
                levels = c("Mass", "Premium", "Luxury", "Top luxury", "Bespoke")),
  prominence = c(30, 55, 78, 52, 18)
)
ggplot(tiers, aes(tier, prominence, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["blue"]], size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 3, y = 86, label = "Loud signals\n(medium types separate from low)", size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.8, y = 36, label = "Quiet signals\n(countersignaling)", size = 3.2,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Price tier", y = "Logo / brand prominence (index)",
       title = "Brand prominence is not monotonic in price",
       caption = "Stylised pattern consistent with Han, Nunes, & Dreze (2010) and Feltovich et al. (2002); not empirical data.")
```

## Chapter Summary {#information-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- Information asymmetry can unravel markets through **adverse selection**
  [@akerlof1970]; remedies include signals, screens, certification, and disclosure.
- A **signal** is a chosen, observable action whose cost is lower for high-quality
  types; without differential cost, it cannot separate types [@spence1973].
- Effective signals are **observable, costly to fake, consistent, and fit** the
  hidden attribute [@connelly2010].
- **Screening** inverts the logic: the uninformed party designs a menu so that
  types self-select [@rothschild1976].
- **Costly signaling** and **identity signaling** extend the theory to status and
  social identity; tastes catch on and die out as signals diffuse [@Berger_2007].
- **Countersignaling** explains why the highest types sometimes refuse to signal
  [@feltovich2002; @han2010].
:::

## Discussion Questions {#information-questions}

1. Spence's model implies that education can be valuable even if it teaches
   nothing. What evidence would distinguish a signaling account from a
   human-capital account of the college wage premium?
2. Choose a product category you know well. List three signals sellers use and
   evaluate each on cost, observability, fit, and consistency.
3. Online reviews are often described as solving the lemons problem. Under what
   conditions might reviews themselves become a pooling signal?
4. Design a screening menu for a B2B software firm with three customer segments.
   How would you test whether the menu is incentive-compatible?
5. When would you predict *countersignaling* in a labour market? Formulate a
   testable hypothesis.
6. A firm announces an ESG certification. What would you need to show to argue
   that the certification is a signal rather than a correlate of firm quality?

## Further Reading {#information-reading}

- @akerlof1970 — the foundational statement of adverse selection; short and readable.
- @spence1973 — the original signaling model; the logic behind every later application.
- @connelly2010 — the standard review of signaling theory in management, with a
  useful construct glossary.
- @kirmani2000 — a marketing-focused review of quality signals and when they work.
- @bergh2014 — a critical assessment of how management research uses (and misuses)
  signaling theory.
- @han2010 — an elegant demonstration of countersignaling in luxury consumption.
- @Berger_2016 — an accessible book on social influence and identity signaling.
